episode_thesis: Brennan argues that price moves because trade impact (not information) sets off reflexive feedback, so markets are path-dependent, non-ergodic, fractal systems in which trends are reinforcing structure that builds across time scales and low volatility is latent compressed risk; Gaussian tools (Sharpe, VaR, Kelly, expectancy) are therefore the wrong toolkit. His response is engineering for survival: behaviourally orthogonal ensembles of trend systems and sizing from closed balance. The host agrees with most of the picture but defends dynamic (volatility-based) sizing as an equally valid, proven design choice, so the episode ends as a polite disagreement on position sizing rather than on trend following itself.

speakers.name: Rich (Richard Brennan)
speakers.role: Australian trend follower and self-styled 'outlier hunter'; regular co-host of the Systematic Investor series
speakers.speaker_note: Identified by content (fractals, closed-balance sizing, outlier hunter) and by the host's address. Ledger labels both speakers by first name; ledger claim C17-1 is attributed to Rich but its text ('even though we use dynamic position sizing I do the same') is Niels speaking, see the Niels entry and gaps.

worldview_premises.premise: Financial markets are not an environment humans evolved in, so rules-based, left-hemisphere processes (and AI) beat discretionary trading, in which emotions such as fear when volatility rises constrain rule-following.
worldview_premises.support: Analogy from McGilchrist and Anil Seth's work on the divided brain; no market evidence.

worldview_premises.premise: Prediction horizons in markets are short, like weather, because of reflexivity; AI will compress them further and defeat itself, favouring trends that arise from structure rather than prediction.
worldview_premises.support: Reflexivity argument and weather analogy; offered as his expectation.

worldview_premises.premise: Price moves because of trade impact (changes in supply and demand), not because information is revealed; each order reshapes conditions for the next, which is what makes markets reflexive and self-modifying.
worldview_premises.support: Bouchaud's microstructure research; reasoning from first principles.

worldview_premises.premise: Market impact is sublinear (square-root law: doubling order size raises impact about 40%) because liquidity is an adaptive, elastic surface; small trades vanish in noise but aligned small trades compound feedback and volatility clusters.
worldview_premises.support: Cites Bouchaud's research on square-root impact.

worldview_premises.premise: Market events are conditional (each changes the probability of the next), so markets are path dependent and non-ergodic; wealth has a lower bound at zero and compounds, so ensemble statistics do not describe an individual path and the Gaussian toolkit (Markowitz, Sharpe, standard deviation, expectancy, risk of ruin) breaks down.
worldview_premises.support: Cites Ole Peters on ergodicity and Mandelbrot; walks through the expectancy equation as an ergodic statistic.

worldview_premises.premise: Returns have fat tails consistent with power laws and fractal behaviour (32 five-sigma events in 30 years in S&P futures versus one per 170,000 years under Gaussian); market memory is better captured by the Hurst exponent and tail properties. He concedes markets may not be exactly fractal.
worldview_premises.support: His own count for ES futures and other liquid markets; Mandelbrot. Hedged: 'the verdict's out'.

worldview_premises.premise: Low volatility is latent, compressed risk (a compressed sponge awaiting a tipping point); volatility is not risk, and standard volatility measures cannot define risk. Live fractal systems show directionless and directional volatility, with or without cross-market correlation.
worldview_premises.support: Physical analogies (conservation of energy, avalanche); no data given.

worldview_premises.premise: Post-GFC quantitative easing and central-bank coordination suppressed trends through compression and buy-the-dip behaviour; the stored energy was released from 2020 like an avalanche; the 2010-2018 period was the anomaly for trend following.
worldview_premises.support: Interpretation of recent market history; no data.

worldview_premises.premise: Fractal structure persists across scales: noise at high resolution becomes rhythm at lower resolution. Short-horizon zigzags cancel (mean reversion), whereas reinforcing directional impacts add up, so trends are visible only as scale lengthens.
worldview_premises.support: Pixels-to-image analogy; no empirical test.

worldview_premises.premise: Mean-reversion strategies earn small linear profits until a negative-skew event causes a nonlinear loss, while trend following takes small linear losses and earns nonlinear gains from outliers.
worldview_premises.support: Description of P&L shapes; no data.

worldview_premises.premise: Positive feedback (buying begets buying) moves price away from equilibrium and creates trends; negative feedback restores balance; markets oscillate between them, with quiet periods punctuated by volatility bursts.
worldview_premises.support: Feedback-system reasoning with a crude-oil cascade example.

worldview_premises.premise: Positive feedback eventually exhausts buyers (valuation stretch, concentration) and flips; reversals release stored energy and are fast and violent, as seen in gold and metals that week. This is renewal, not failure.
worldview_premises.support: Example of the late-October 2025 precious-metals drop.

worldview_premises.premise: Trends can be random, a segment of a mean-reverting cycle, or structural with serial correlation; only the structural kind (outliers) persists, so trends should not be treated as visual patterns. Compression hides structure and expansions (outliers, phase transitions) are where tails dominate and returns are made.
worldview_premises.support: Conceptual argument; no test of how to distinguish the three in real time.

worldview_premises.premise: Markets are non-ergodic with one path and ruin ends the game, so survival (not expectancy) is the true measure of success, including for judging a manager's track record. Kelly, expectancy and value-at-risk are bad statistics because they derive from a Gaussian model.
worldview_premises.support: Ergodicity argument; sequence-risk example (-50% then +50%).

mechanism_chains.topic: From a single trade to trends: impact, reflexive feedback and cascades across scales

steps.to: some cancel, some reinforce through the order book and liquidity network
steps.why: impact changes supply/demand balance for the next trade

steps.to: feedback loop: traders observe price, update models, act again (reflexivity)
steps.why: prices create information as well as reflect it

steps.to: small aligned trades compound; volatility clusters; directional bias emerges
steps.why: small trades vanish alone but add up when aligned

steps.from: scale: tick to hourly to daily to monthly
steps.to: local bursts become clusters, narrative and a systemic move
steps.why: reinforcement persists across scales while short-term zigzags cancel (crude-oil example)

mechanism_chains.evidence: Reasoning from Bouchaud's impact research and a worked crude-oil cascade; no empirical test of the cascade.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: When positive feedback is exhausted (valuation stretch, concentration), it flips and unwinds quickly.

steps.to: buyers exhausted, valuation stretched, risk concentrated
steps.why: the alignment that built the trend becomes its constraint

steps.to: selling accelerates, stop-losses trigger, margin calls force unwinding
steps.why: energy stored through the long build is released

steps.to: system renewal and the cycle restarts (reinforcement, alignment, reversal)

mechanism_chains.evidence: Illustrated with the gold and metals reversal of that week.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Not stated; timing of exhaustion is not predictable in his framework.

steps.from: QE and coordinated central-bank action, stable inflation
steps.to: trend suppression, compression and buy-the-dip behaviour
steps.why: central banks succeeded in keeping inflation low and stable
compression hides structure; the risk never went away

steps.to: explosion out of compression and strong trends
steps.why: the system flipped out of the compressed state

steps.to: less correlation and a more favourable trend environment ('trend heaven') unless policy whipsaw returns
steps.why: different challenges per central bank; policy reversals create whipsaw

mechanism_chains.fails_when: Frequent policy changes create whipsaw ('death by a thousand cuts'), as in the first six months of 2025.

mechanism_chains.topic: Path dependence, survival and closed-balance sizing

steps.from: non-ergodic wealth with a floor at zero
steps.to: expectancy and risk-of-ruin formulas mislead; order of wins and losses decides outcome
steps.why: same expectancy can end in ruin or compounding depending on sequence

steps.to: losses shrink the base and the drag compounds (-50% then +50% leaves a permanent hole)
steps.why: every trade changes the base from which the next grows

steps.from: size new positions from closed balance (realized capital)
steps.to: exposure falls automatically in drawdowns and scales up only after confirmed gains
steps.why: closed balance embeds the drawdowns and recoveries already experienced

steps.from: large positions on a positive-expectancy system
steps.to: compounding drag and ruin, whereas very small positions let a 2%-expectancy system compound
steps.why: geometric growth depends on size relative to capital

mechanism_chains.evidence: Worked examples (5% expectancy with large size goes to zero; 30% win rate, 3:1 payoff, 2% expectancy with small size compounds well); stated by Brennan without displayed backtests.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Not stated; the host raises issues with inception-date dependence and inflows (see disagreements).

mechanism_chains.topic: AI will shorten prediction horizons and favour trend

steps.from: AI is backward-looking pattern recognition that predicts forward
steps.to: more participants acting on short-horizon predictions
prediction horizon compresses further and AI defeats its own purpose
steps.why: acting on predictions changes the market

steps.to: more weight on structural alignment and concerted directional behaviour, which favours trend
steps.why: trends rest on structure rather than prediction

mechanism_chains.evidence: Speculative; the host recalls well-known managers saying AI is far from producing alpha.

decision_process.practice: Do not define a trend as a visual pattern; hunt for structural outliers (serial-correlation phase transitions) using families of systems that listen for different ways structure can express itself.
decision_process.why: Only structural trends persist; random trends and segments of mean-reverting cycles do not.

decision_process.practice: Stay a medium-to-long-term trend follower rather than trade shorter horizons.
decision_process.why: Shorter time frames are more mean reverting (cancellation), while institutions' interaction at medium to long horizons reinforces trends.

decision_process.practice: Run ensembles of trend systems diversified by behaviour (breakout, volatility expansion, smooth persistence, mean-reversion-into-trend), not by correlation.
decision_process.why: Correlation is fickle; structural outliers can take many forms and the systems will never all act in concert; readiness rather than prediction.

decision_process.practice: Size new positions from closed (realized) balance, not floating equity.
decision_process.why: It automatically reduces exposure in drawdown and scales up only after confirmed gains; with positive skew it keeps open equity above closed balance, so sizing is more conservative.

decision_process.practice: Keep individual position sizes small even when expectancy is positive.
decision_process.why: Large sizes on a 5% positive expectancy produce compounding drag and ruin; small sizes on a 2% expectancy system compound well.

decision_process.practice: Do not use volatility or other statistical risk measures to protect the portfolio; protect through robust, resilient, non-overfit system design and sizing (engineer the bridge, don't blame the weather).
decision_process.why: Their assumptions come from a Gaussian world.

decision_process.practice: Judge managers and systems by survival.
decision_process.why: One path; ruin ends the game.

decision_process.practice: Stick to the process through bad stretches (the poor first six months of 2025); deeper understanding of why trends occur raises comfort with the method.
decision_process.why: Policy whipsaw was an environment effect, not a model failure.

decision_process.practice: Present oneself as a distinct type of trend follower with specific objectives; allocators should select among types by objective.
decision_process.why: Varieties differ in philosophy and the conversation is gaining traction among allocators.

speakers.evidence_style: First-principles and analogy (brain hemispheres, weather, bridges, avalanche, pixels), appeal to academic authorities (Bouchaud, Peters, Mandelbrot), a few own counts (32 five-sigma events in ES) and stylised worked examples of expectancy and size. No displayed backtests of the closed-balance claims.

current_views.view: Bullish on trend following: a robust environment after a difficult first six months of 2025 with policy whipsaw; expects to finish the year strong.
current_views.reasoning: Markets are reasserting themselves, policy whipsaw has faded, solid trends are appearing.

current_views.view: Decoupled, less coordinated central banks make this 'trend heaven' provided everyday policy changes do not cause whipsaw.
current_views.reasoning: Post-GFC to 2018 was the anomaly; decoupling means less correlation and buy-the-dip fading.

current_views.view: Trend models are turning long in energies; metals may take a breather but systems stay active in metals.
current_views.reasoning: Model positioning after the metals' retracement.

current_views.view: Buy-the-dip, a behavioural by-product of compression, is expected to fade.
AI adoption will shorten prediction horizons further, which favours trend following.
The sharp precious-metals reversal that week is feedback inverting, with energy released quickly.
current_views.reasoning: Positive feedback exhausted after a long rise.

speakers.name: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
speakers.role: Host (Top Traders Unplugged); veteran hedge fund manager who uses dynamic (volatility-based) position sizing
speakers.speaker_note: Host questions are context; mapped as a speaker because he argues a position on position sizing and reports market data. Ledger C17-1 (constant sizing in a big trend helps but constant sizing in all other positions can detract) is attributed to 'Rich' in the ledger, but the text shows Niels: he says 'even though we use dynamic position sizing I do the same' and 'we both want the long longer trend'. C17-2 is shared (Rich on distinguishing himself, Niels recalling a prior discussion of types of trend follower); the last sentence may be either speaker.

worldview_premises.premise: The stability of inflation, not only its level, strongly shapes the markets trend followers trade; central banks succeeded in keeping inflation low and stable, which Brennan links to the compression period.
worldview_premises.support: His own reflection ('people, myself included, have underestimated'); ledger correction: this point is Niels', not Rich's.

worldview_premises.premise: Dynamic (volatility-based) position sizing and closed-balance sizing are different design choices, not right versus wrong: most managers use dynamic sizing and long track records show no big difference in returns.
worldview_premises.support: Observation of 20 to 40-year track records and survival of dynamic-sizing managers over 25 to 30 years.

worldview_premises.premise: For liquid futures managers who can liquidate in 24 hours, open equity is not illusory, so sizing from full equity is reasonable.
worldview_premises.support: Liquidity of the markets traded.

worldview_premises.premise: Closed-balance sizing depends on the inception date: in a fund with ongoing client inflows investors enter at different points, which leaves undefined risk for those not at inception; it also reduces volatility by sizing on a smaller equity, just as dynamic sizing does.
worldview_premises.support: Logical objection; no data.

worldview_premises.premise: Constant position sizing may help in a big trend (gold, cocoa) but the same sizing across all other positions can detract; both approaches have worked for decades.
worldview_premises.support: Experience; ledger attributed to Rich but the speaker is Niels.

worldview_premises.premise: AI is far from producing alpha (as recalled from well-known hedge fund managers), with gains mainly in programming efficiency.
worldview_premises.support: Hearsay recall (possibly Ken Griffin or Paul Tudor Jones); he is unsure of the names.

worldview_premises.premise: Electricity is the successor to oil as the core input to growth; shortages of power, cooling and grid raise inflation and stall productivity. Oil has been flat for a long time despite Middle East disruptions, yet most observers still anchor on oil.
worldview_premises.support: Quoting a former Saxo chief strategist; he is 'not so sure' the world looks at it that way.

worldview_premises.premise: Mixing mean-reversion-into-trend and breakout systems in an orthogonal ensemble makes Brennan 'less classic' than what allocators expect from a trend follower.
worldview_premises.support: His observation about allocator expectations.

worldview_premises.premise: Post-GFC difficulty for trend following was limited to a few years (about 2018 to 2020), with good years such as 2014 in between, so it was not a decade-long failure.
worldview_premises.support: Recollection of track records.

decision_process.practice: Use dynamic (volatility-based) position sizing from full equity; view it as proven after 25 to 30 years of survival, more complex than closed-balance sizing but not wrong.
decision_process.why: Open equity is liquid; the track records of dynamic sizers show no big difference in returns; the closed-balance approach also reduces volatility and has discretionary elements (the cutback rule).

decision_process.practice: Weigh holding constant size in a big trend against the drag from constant size in all other positions.
decision_process.why: Both have worked; there are pros and cons.

decision_process.practice: Use the Trend Barometer (52 and rising, a strong reading) as a gauge of how favourable the environment is for trend followers.
decision_process.why: A strong reading is consistent with positive CTA returns.

speakers.evidence_style: Industry experience and observation of long track records; reports index data and market news; does not present tests.

current_views.view: Trend environment is constructive: metals correcting but trending, equities well behaved, soft commodities (sugar, coffee, cotton) a new return source, energies and currencies range-bound; but daily volatility of CTA returns is higher.
current_views.reasoning: Observation of manager returns he can see daily, including his own; big precious-metals swings may mark a short-term top correction.

current_views.view: Precious-metals volatility exploded: gold fell over 6% in a day (largest drop in over a decade), silver and platinum more, palladium -16% in two days, with implications for position sizing.
New US sanctions on Russian oil companies lifted crude about 5% intraday, an example of an exogenous event that can start an energy trend.
Private credit problems may reflect a new market acronym, 'DADT' (don't ask, don't think).
current_views.reasoning: His interpretation of the Saxo strategist's note.

current_views.view: Trend barometer 52; BTOP50 +2.12% in October (+2.58% YTD), SG CTA +2.35% (-0.4% YTD), SG Trend +2.85% (+0.53% YTD), short-term traders about +1% October and about -4% YTD; MSCI World +18.3%, US aggregate bonds +9.8%, S&P 500 TR +15.08% YTD.

disagreements.topic: Position sizing: closed-balance versus dynamic (volatility-based) sizing

positions.speaker: Rich (Richard Brennan)
positions.position: Size from closed balance because it is realized, survivable capital; it cuts exposure in drawdowns, avoids ruin and embeds humility; volatility and Gaussian measures are unsound and shouldn't be used for protection.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Neither is right or wrong; dynamic sizing is used by most managers and has survived 25 to 30 years; closed-balance sizing also reduces volatility and has discretionary cutback rules; open equity is liquid so full-equity sizing is reasonable; inflows break the inception-date logic.

positions.speaker: Rich (Richard Brennan)
positions.position: Closed balance is the only equity you actually possess; unrealised equity is illusory and larger sizes on it start leveraging up toward an unfavourable compounded path.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: For liquid futures portfolios that can be liquidated in 24 hours, open equity is not illusory.

disagreements.topic: Constant versus dynamic sizing in big trends

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Constant size in a big winner like gold or cocoa may help, but constant size across all other positions can detract; invites a less black-and-white view.

positions.speaker: Rich (Richard Brennan)
positions.position: Distinguishes himself as an outlier hunter with a distinctive philosophy and specific objectives; does not claim all trend followers need the same objectives.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Brennan asserts closed-balance sizing is 'a structural response to a non-ergodic environment' but shows no backtest, drawdown or return comparison against dynamic sizing; the 5% and 2% expectancy examples are stylised.

The claim that positive skew keeps open equity above closed balance (so sizing is more conservative) is true only after inception and in profit; Niels' point that fund investors enter at different times is not answered on air.

Brennan rejects volatility as a risk measure yet describes low volatility as latent risk; his view requires telling compression apart from calm in real time, which is not specified, and his own ensemble uses volatility-expansion detection.
The 32 five-sigma events in 30 years of ES futures depends on how sigma is estimated (volatility window, overlapping events); no method is given, and clustering may inflate the count.

Brennan says the fractal verdict is out but then treats fractal structure as the foundation of the trend explanation; the cascade-across-scales argument (crude oil example) is narrative, not demonstrated.

Brennan sees post-GFC compression and the 2020 explosion as the cause of trend failure and recovery, while the host notes that the poor period was only a few years (2018 to 2020) and 2014 was strong; the timing of compression and 'anomaly' is therefore loose.

The AI claim (AI adoption shortens prediction horizons and favours trend; AI has 'evolved in financial markets') is speculation; the host's counter (leading managers say AI is far from alpha) is hearsay with uncertain names.
Ledger attribution error: C17-1 is attributed to Rich but is spoken by Niels (dynamic-sizing manager). C06-1 is already corrected to Niels in the ledger.
The Saxo strategist's electricity thesis and the 'DADT' interpretation are reported second-hand; neither speaker ties them to a trend signal.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Brennan's observable inputs for future trend profits: whether central banks stay decoupled and uncoordinated (less correlation, no buy-the-dip), absence of frequent policy reversals (whipsaw), presence of directional versus directionless volatility and cross-market correlation (live compress-and-expand structure), and exhaustion signs in positive-feedback trends (stretched valuation, concentration) preceding fast reversals. Horizon is medium to long term; short horizons are expected to remain mean reverting. The host adds the Trend Barometer, soft-commodity returns, and the electricity/energy-policy shocks (sanctions on Russian oil) as trend starters. Neither gives price forecasts; both state they are not predicting.
reader_inferences: (reader) The core logic is a feedback-structure argument: trade impact creates reflexive feedback, reinforcement survives at longer scales while short-term moves cancel, so trend profits come from rare structural expansions after compression; the sizing dispute follows from non-ergodicity, not from signal design.

(reader) The two sizing approaches differ mainly in what they react to: closed balance responds to realized drawdown (slow, path-based), dynamic sizing responds to measured volatility (fast); the host's point that both reduce volatility suggests the empirical gap should be small, consistent with his reading of long track records.

(reader) Brennan's 'volatility is not risk' and 'low volatility is latent risk' imply that volatility-targeted books mechanically enlarge positions into compression, the same point he and Dredge make in the later episode MT224, but here it is not tested.

(reader) The behaviourally orthogonal ensemble (breakout, volatility expansion, smooth persistence, mean-reversion-into-trend) is a form of model diversification meant to hedge uncertainty about which trend structure will occur.
